title: Latency & Throughput
subtitle: Watch one service answer requests, then see why averages lie, tails hurt, and Little's Law predicts overload.
learn: The difference between latency, throughput, and bandwidth
Why p50 and p99 tell different stories and the average hides both
How fan-out turns a rare slow call into a common slow page
How to use Little's Law (L = λ × W) to size concurrency and spot overload

steps.title: Fast, or fast enough?
steps.body: Your service feels quick when you test it alone. Then launch day comes, thousands of users arrive, and some of them wait several seconds. Nothing is broken. You are simply measuring the wrong thing, or only one of the several things that make a system feel fast.
steps.idea: Speed is not one number: how long one request takes and how many you can handle are different questions.
steps.caption: A service sits between many clients and its backends.

steps.title: Latency: one request's wait
steps.body: Latency is the time one request takes from being sent to being answered. Here a client call goes through the load balancer, the app checks the cache, and returns. Assume the whole trip takes 40 ms. Latency is measured per request, in milliseconds, and users feel it directly.
steps.idea: Latency is how long one request waits; lower is better and users feel it.
steps.caption: One request, 40 ms start to finish.

steps.title: Throughput: requests per second
steps.body: Throughput is how many requests the system completes each second. If each request takes 40 ms and the app handles 20 at the same time, it finishes about 20 / 0.04 = 500 requests per second. Latency and throughput are related but separate: you can raise throughput by doing more work in parallel without making any single request faster.
steps.idea: Throughput is the count of completed requests per second; parallelism raises it without cutting latency.
steps.caption: Many requests flow through at once: 500 per second.

steps.title: Bandwidth is the pipe, not the speed
steps.body: Bandwidth is the maximum data a link can carry per second, such as 1 Gbit/s. It sets an upper bound on throughput for large responses, but a fat pipe does not shorten the trip. A 1 KB reply on a 10 Gbit/s link and on a 100 Mbit/s link both take about 40 ms in total, almost all of it delay (network round trip plus server work), not transfer time (the 1 KB transfer takes about 0.08 ms even on 100 Mbit/s). Bandwidth matters when the payload is big, latency when it is small.
steps.idea: Bandwidth is capacity, latency is delay; a wider pipe barely makes a small message arrive sooner.
steps.caption: A wide pipe still waits for the round trip.

steps.title: Percentiles beat averages
steps.body: Latency varies from request to request, so one number cannot describe it. The p50 (median) is the value half of requests beat: 40 ms here. The p99 is the value 99% of requests beat, so the slowest 1% take longer: about 400 ms here. If 99% of requests take 40 ms and 1% take 400 ms, the average is about 44 ms and hides the slow ones entirely. Report percentiles alongside the mean, never the mean alone.
steps.idea: p50 shows the typical request, p99 shows the slowest 1%; the average hides both.
steps.caption: Most requests are fast; a few are ten times slower.

steps.title: Why the tail exists
steps.body: Slow outliers have ordinary causes: a garbage collection (GC) pause, a noisy neighbour (another tenant hogging the shared host), a cold cache miss that hits the database, a retry after packet loss, or a lock held by another query. They are rare per request, but they never fully go away. The slow end of the distribution is called tail latency.
steps.idea: Tail latency comes from many small, random stalls; you manage it, you cannot eliminate it.
steps.caption: A cache miss sends one request down the slow path.

steps.title: Fan-out multiplies the tail
steps.body: A single page often calls many backends. Suppose each call has a 1% chance of being slow (its per-call p99 is 400 ms), the calls are independent, and a page waits on 20 of them in parallel. The chance that at least one is slow is 1 - 0.99^20, about 18%. So a backend's p99 becomes roughly your page's p82. The more calls per request, the more the tail dominates what users see.
steps.idea: With N parallel calls, the page is only as fast as its slowest one, so rare slowness becomes common.
steps.caption: 3 of the 20 calls shown: the app waits on every backend, so one slow reply delays all.

steps.title: Little's Law
steps.body: Little's Law says the average number of requests in the system equals the arrival rate times the average time each spends there: L = λ × W. At 500 req/s and 0.04 s each, L = 500 × 0.04 = 20 requests in flight. W is the average time in system, not the median (about 44 ms by the earlier numbers, so L is roughly 22; we use 40 ms to keep the arithmetic round). It holds for any stable system and needs no assumptions about the distribution. Use it to size thread pools, connection pools, and queues, and size them above the average L for headroom, since real concurrency fluctuates.
steps.idea: In-flight requests = arrival rate × time in system, so latency and concurrency are linked.
steps.caption: 500 req/s × 0.04 s = 20 requests in flight.

steps.title: Latency rises, the pool runs out
steps.body: Now the database slows and each request takes 400 ms. Same 500 req/s arrive, so you would need L = 500 × 0.4 = 200 requests in flight. But 50 worker threads can finish only 50 / 0.4 = 125 requests per second. The other 375 per second pile up in the queue (only 50 can be in service at once; the rest wait) until it fills or clients time out (assume a 2 s timeout, so most requests wait in the queue until then). Arrivals exceed the 125/s the pool can finish, so the queue grows; clients that time out often retry, adding even more load. Slowness spreads and can topple the service.
steps.idea: When W grows at a fixed arrival rate, concurrency explodes past capacity and queues feed on themselves.
steps.caption: Need 200 in flight, have 50 slots: 375 req/s pile up.

steps.title: What to remember
steps.body: Latency is one request's wait, throughput is requests completed per second, and bandwidth is the pipe's capacity. Track p50 and p99, never only the average, and expect fan-out to make tails matter more. Use L = λ × W to check that your pools cover your latency. To protect the tail, add timeouts, cache hot data, bound queues, and shed load (reject excess requests early) before queues grow.
steps.idea: Measure percentiles, watch concurrency with Little's Law, and design for the tail.
steps.caption: Healthy service: fast median, bounded tail, enough slots.

quiz.q: A link is upgraded from 100 Mbit/s to 10 Gbit/s. Users loading a tiny 2 KB JSON response from a server 80 ms away barely notice. Why?
options: The 80 ms round trip dominates; the payload was already tiny, so more capacity saves almost nothing
Faster links increase latency for small messages
JSON is compressed automatically so link speed is irrelevant
quiz.why: Bandwidth is capacity. For a 2 KB reply the transfer time is a fraction of a millisecond; the round-trip delay is what the user waits on.

quiz.q: Your dashboard shows average latency of 60 ms, but users complain about occasional multi-second hangs. What should you add first?
quiz.why: The mean is dominated by the many fast requests and hides rare slow ones. Percentiles like p99 expose the tail users are complaining about.

quiz.q: A page makes 50 independent parallel backend calls, each with a 99th-percentile latency of 300 ms and a typical latency of 30 ms. About how often will the page wait roughly 300 ms or more?
quiz.why: The chance at least one of 50 calls is slow is 1 - 0.99^50, about 40%. Fan-out makes a backend's tail the page's common case.

quiz.q: A service gets 200 requests per second and the average request spends 250 ms inside it. About how many requests are in flight on average?
quiz.why: Little's Law: L = λ × W = 200 × 0.25 = 50 requests in flight, so you need at least that many worker slots plus headroom.

quiz.q: Traffic is steady at 300 req/s, but a dependency slows and your average time per request triples. With a fixed pool sized with only modest headroom over the original load, what happens?
options: Throughput rises because workers stay busy
Nothing, because arrival rate did not change
Needed concurrency triples, so the pool saturates, queues form, and latency climbs further
Latency drops because fewer requests finish
quiz.why: L = λ × W, so tripling W triples required concurrency. Once it exceeds the pool, requests queue, which raises W again and worsens the overload.

cheatsheet.def: Time for one request to complete, from send to response. Measured in milliseconds; lower is better.
Requests (or bytes) completed per second. Raised by parallelism, caching, and efficiency, not only by faster single requests.
Maximum data a link can move per second. It caps throughput for big payloads but does not reduce the round-trip delay.
The value that 50% / 95% / 99% of requests beat. p50 is the typical case; p99 means 1 in 100 requests is slower.
The slow end of the latency distribution (p99 and beyond), caused by GC pauses, cache misses, retries, and contention.
With N parallel calls, P(at least one slow) = 1 - (1 - p)^N. A 1% tail across 20 calls hits about 18% of pages.
L = λ × W: average in-flight requests = arrival rate × average time in system. Use it to size pools and queues.

Hedged request: after a short delay, send a duplicate to another replica and use the first answer (for safe/idempotent reads; costs extra load). Load shedding: reject excess requests early so the rest stay fast. Also timeouts, bounded queues.
